docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from gbq import BigQuery

# BigQuery project id as listed in the Google Developers Console.
project_id = 'project_id'

# BigQuery dataset id as listed in the Google Developers Console.
dataset_id = 'dataset_id'

# BigQuery table/view id as listed in the Google Developers Console.
structure_id = 'structure_id'

# BigQuery structure definition as defined in the Google Developers Console.
json_schema = {
    "type": "table",
    "schema": [{"name": "id", "type": "INTEGER", "mode": "REQUIRED"}],
}

# Authenticates with Application Default Credentials: Workload Identity, an attached
# service account, GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS, or `gcloud auth application-default login`.
bq = BigQuery(project=project_id)

bq.create_or_update_structure(project_id, dataset_id, structure_id, json_schema)

docs.title: Updating Existing Tables
docs.text:
create_or_update_structure creates the structure if it doesn't exist. Otherwise it updates it to match the definition, and skips the API call when nothing changed:

  • The definition is the source of truth. Labels, description and clustering that the definition omits are removed from the existing table or view.
  • Schema fields keep every attribute in the definition, such as policyTags, precision and maxLength.
  • BigQuery cannot change an existing table's partitioning, except a time partition's expiration. If the definition's partitioning differs in any other way, InvalidDefinitionException is raised and the table is left unchanged; recreate the table to change it.

docs.title: Stored Procedures
docs.text:
A definition with a body creates or updates a SQL stored procedure. The body can be a string or a list of lines, and each argument's data_type can be any BigQuery type, including ARRAY<...> and STRUCT<...>:

procedure = {
    "body": [
        "INSERT INTO `project_id.dataset_id.events` (user_id, tags)",
        "SELECT user.id, tags FROM UNNEST([user])",
    ],
    "arguments": [
        {"name": "user", "data_type": "STRUCT<id INT64, name STRING>"},
        {"name": "tags", "data_type": "ARRAY<STRING>"},
    ],
    "description": "Records an event for a user",
}

bq.create_or_update_structure(project_id, dataset_id, "record_event", procedure)

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
BigQuery uses Application Default Credentials unless you pass credentials explicitly. Prefer this, or a google.auth credentials object, over long-lived service account keys:

import google.auth
from google.auth import impersonated_credentials

source, _ = google.auth.default()
credentials = impersonated_credentials.Credentials(
    source_credentials=source,
    target_principal="deployer@project_id.iam.gserviceaccount.com",
    target_scopes=["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/bigquery"],
)
bq = BigQuery(project=project_id, credentials=credentials)

# A service account key as a JSON string is still supported
bq = BigQuery(svc_account=key_json, project=project_id)

docs.title: Running Queries
docs.text:
Pass values as query parameters instead of formatting them into the SQL string, so they can't change the query (SQL injection):

from google.cloud import bigquery

job = bq.execute(
    "SELECT * FROM `project_id.dataset_id.users` WHERE name = @name",
    query_parameters=[bigquery.ScalarQueryParameter("name", "STRING", user_input)],
)
rows = list(job.result())

docs.text: To learn the basics of how to start using gbq, read the Getting Started page.

docs.text:

docs.title: BigQuery
docs.text:
BigQueryUtil represent a BigQuery Util resource.

Authentication uses, in order of precedence: credentials, then svc_account, then Application Default Credentials (for example Workload Identity, an attached service account, GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS, or gcloud auth application-default login). Prefer credentials or Application Default Credentials over long-lived service account keys.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default svc_account Optional[str]

Stringified JSON service account key.

None project Optional[str]

Project bound to the operation.

None credentials Optional[Credentials]

Credentials to use, e.g. from google.auth.default() or impersonation.

None

Raises:

Type Description GbqException

If both svc_account and credentials are given, or if svc_account is not a valid service account key.

docs.title: create_or_update_structure(project, dataset, structure_id, json_schema)
docs.text:
Function creates/updates provided json schema to the structure.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default project str

Project bound to the operation.

required dataset str

ID of dataset containing the structure.

required structure_id str

ID of the structure.

required json_schema Union[List[Dict], Dict]

Raw JSON schema of the table. If List[Dict] it is assumed that the value is table schema, if Dict than value can include partitioning scheme, clustering, table schema, view query, labels, etc

required

Examples:

List[Dict]: [ { "name": "name1", "type: "INTEGER", "mode: "REQUIRED" }, { "name": "name2", "type: "STRING" }... ]

Dict: List[Dict]: { "clustering": ["name"], "partition": { "type": "time", "definition": { "type": "DAY" } }, "description": "this is a partitioned table", "labels": {"team: "abc"}, "schema: [ { "name": "name1", "type: "INTEGER", "mode: "REQUIRED" }, { "name": "name2", "type: "STRING" }... ] }

Returns:

Name Type Description Table Table | Routine

An object of BigQuery Table.

docs.title: execute(query, query_parameters=None, job_config=None, *, project=None)
docs.text:
Function return a QueryJob object after executing a SQL statement

Pass untrusted values as query_parameters and reference them in the query as @name, rather than formatting them into the query string, to avoid SQL injection.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default query str

BigQuery query string

required query_parameters Optional[Sequence[QueryParameter]]

Parameters referenced by the query, e.g. bigquery.ScalarQueryParameter("name", "STRING", value).

None job_config Optional[QueryJobConfig]

Extra job settings such as labels, dry_run or maximum_bytes_billed. It is not modified; query_parameters replace any parameters it already has.

None project Optional[str]

Project to run (and bill) the query job in. Defaults to the project the BigQuery object was created with. Tables in other projects can still be queried by their fully qualified names.

None

Examples:

bq.execute( "SELECT * FROM project.dataset.users WHERE name = @name", query_parameters=[ bigquery.ScalarQueryParameter("name", "STRING", user_input) ], )

Returns:

Type Description QueryJob

QueryJob An object of QueryJob.

docs.title: fetch_rows(query, query_parameters=None, job_config=None, max_results=None, *, project=None)
docs.text:
Function runs a SQL statement and returns its rows.

Unlike execute(), this uses the BigQuery jobs.query fast path, which runs short queries in a single request and returns the first page of rows with the response, instead of creating a job and polling it. Use execute() when you need the QueryJob (job ID, statistics, destination table); use this when you only need the rows.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default query str

BigQuery query string

required query_parameters Optional[Sequence[QueryParameter]]

Parameters referenced by the query as @name; see execute().

None job_config Optional[QueryJobConfig]

Extra job settings; see execute(). It is not modified.

None max_results Optional[int]

Maximum number of rows to return.

None project Optional[str]

Project to run (and bill) the query in; see execute().

None

Returns:

Name Type Description RowIterator RowIterator

The query's rows.

docs.title: get_table_in_project(project, max_workers=8)
docs.text:
Function returns list of TableListItem objects of all the tables and views in a project.

Tables are listed for up to max_workers datasets concurrently, instead of one dataset at a time, so a project with many datasets takes a fraction of the time.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default project str

Project bound to the operation.

required max_workers int

Maximum number of datasets to list tables for at once. The default stays below the HTTP connection pool size of the underlying client.

8

Returns:

Type Description list[TableListItem]

List[TableListItem]: A list of object of BigQuery TableListItem, grouped by dataset in the order the datasets are listed.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Support for Python 3.15
  • BigQuery(credentials=...) accepts any google.auth credentials object, and svc_account is now optional: without either, Application Default Credentials are used
  • execute() accepts query_parameters (use these instead of formatting values into SQL) and a job_config

  • delete_dataset() accepts delete_contents

  • fetch_rows() runs a query through the BigQuery jobs.query fast path and returns its rows, avoiding job creation and polling for short queries

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
• get_table_in_project() lists tables for up to 8 datasets concurrently (configurable with max_workers) instead of one dataset at a time
  • delete_dataset() and delete_table_or_view() make one API call instead of two
  • create_or_update_structure() skips the update call when an existing table or view already matches the definition, and otherwise sends only the fields that changed. This also avoids BigQuery's per-table metadata update rate limit when a pipeline re-applies unchanged definitions

docs.title: Security
docs.text: • An invalid svc_account now raises GbqException instead of json.JSONDecodeError or ValueError, without chaining the original error, whose doc attribute held the full key

docs.title: Removed
docs.text: • Support for Python 3.10, which reached end of life on 2026-10-01

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Breaking: delete_dataset() no longer deletes the tables, views and routines in a dataset unless you pass delete_contents=True. By default BigQuery now refuses to delete a non-empty dataset
  • gbq.__version__ is read from the installed package's metadata, so pyproject.toml is the single source of the version. It is 0.0.0+unknown when gbq is imported from source without being installed
  • Releases are made only through hyper-bump-it version bump pull requests; the unused release-please configuration was removed, and the development guide describes the flow
  • When create_or_update_structure() updates an existing table or view, the definition is now the source of truth: labels, description and clustering that the definition omits are removed. Previously they could be set but never cleared
  • Updating an existing table whose partitioning differs from the definition now raises InvalidDefinitionException instead of silently ignoring the partitioning. A changed time partition expiration is applied, since BigQuery allows that in place
  • Methods that take a project argument no longer change the client's default project as a side effect. Previously, execute() ran its job in whichever project the last such call used; it now runs in the project BigQuery was created with, or in the project passed with the new project= argument (also on fetch_rows())
  • Upgraded pydantic to 2.14.1 and google-crc32c to 1.9.0, which ship Python 3.15 wheels
  • Development dependencies moved from requirements*.txt and requirements.lock to [dependency-groups] in pyproject.toml, locked in uv.lock for every supported Python
  • CI, the devbox image and distribution builds now install a pinned uv instead of an unpinned install script, pip install build and a third-party mypy action
  • Invalid structure definitions now raise InvalidDefinitionException instead of a raw KeyError (unknown partition, time or argument types) or a later AttributeError (a definition that is not a dict or list)

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The documentation's changelog page showed the text ../CHANGELOG.md instead of the changelog, and the API reference page was missing. Both are restored
  • Merging a version bump pull request did not release: the workflow needed a personal access token that wasn't configured. It now creates the release with the workflow's own token and starts the publish workflow itself
  • Stored procedure arguments of type ARRAY or STRUCT were sent without an element type or fields, which BigQuery rejects. data_type now accepts full BigQuery types such as ARRAY<INT64> and STRUCT<id INT64, tags ARRAY<STRING>>, and invalid types raise InvalidDefinitionException. JSON and INTERVAL arguments are also supported
  • Schema conversion kept only name, type, mode, description and nested fields, dropping attributes such as policyTags, precision, scale, maxLength and defaultValueExpression. Updates therefore always rewrote the schema and stripped policy tags set on columns. All attributes are now kept, and STRUCT columns get their nested fields like RECORD columns
  • get_table_in_project() is annotated as returning TableListItem objects, which is what it has always returned, instead of Table
  • from gbq import * raised TypeError; __all__ now lists BigQuery, GbqException and InvalidDefinitionException, which are also importable from gbq directly
  • get_bq_schema_from_record duplicated the previous field or raised UnboundLocalError for None values; nulls now map to a NULLABLE STRING field, and unsupported value types raise InvalidDefinitionException
  • Parsing a structure definition no longer mutates the caller's input dictionaries

docs.title: Development Guide
docs.text:
Welcome! Thank you for wanting to make the project better. This section provides an overview on how repository structure and how to work with the code base.

Before you dive into this, it is best to read:

  • The Code of Conduct
  • The Contributing guide

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
The GBQ project uses Docker to ease setting up a consistent development environment. The Docker documentation has details on how to install docker on your computer.

Once that is configured, the test suite can be run locally:

docker compose run --rm test

If you want to be able to execute code in the container:

docker compose run --rm devbox
(your code here)

In the devbox environment you'll be able to enter a python shell and import gbq or any dependencies.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
The docker container has pdb++ install that can be used as a debugger. (However, you are welcome to set up a different debugger if you would like.)

This allows you to easily create a breakpoint anywhere in the code.

def my_function():
    breakpoint()
    ...

When your the code, you will drop into an interactive pdb++ debugger.

See the documentation on pdb and pdb++ for more information.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
You'll be unable to merge code unless the linting and tests pass. You can run these in your container via:

docker compose run --rm test

This will run the same tests, linting, and code coverage that are run by the CI pipeline. The only difference is that, when run locally, ruff is configured to automatically fix issues it detects (with the --format-code flag).

Generally we should endeavor to write tests for every feature. Every new feature branch should increase the test coverage rather than decreasing it.

We use pytest as our testing framework.

docs.title: Stages
docs.text:
To customize / override a specific testing stage, please read the documentation specific to that tool:

  1. PyTest
  2. MyPy
  3. Ruff
  4. Bandit

docs.title: Building the Library
docs.text: gbq is PEP 517 compliant. uv is used as the frontend tool for building the library (uv build), and Hatchling is the build backend. pyproject.toml contains the library metadata.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
All dependencies are declared in pyproject.toml and managed with uv:

  • [project] dependencies - Runtime dependencies of the library, installed by anyone who installs gbq.
  • [dependency-groups] - Development dependencies, pinned to exact versions:
    • test - the test suite and lints
    • docs - building and publishing the documentation
    • dev - everything in test and docs, plus local debugging tools. This is the default group.
  • uv.lock - The fully resolved lock file for every supported Python version. CI and the devbox install from it with uv sync --locked, which fails if it is out of date with pyproject.toml.

After changing dependencies in pyproject.toml, update the lock file and rebuild the devbox:

docker compose run --rm lock
docker compose build devbox

To upgrade every locked dependency to its latest allowed version, run docker compose run --rm lock --upgrade. Renovate also opens a weekly lock file maintenance pull request that does this.

docs.title: Publishing a New Version
docs.text:
Releases are made by merging a version bump pull request created with hyper-bump-it. The version lives in pyproject.toml; gbq.__version__ is read from the installed package's metadata.

  1. Make sure the ## [Unreleased] section of CHANGELOG.md describes everything in the release, marking breaking changes. The bump turns it into the new version's section, and that section becomes the GitHub release notes.
  2. Start with a local clone of the repo on the default branch with a clean working tree, and have uv installed.

  3. Bump the version by part (major, minor, or patch), for example:

    uv run hyper-bump-it by minor

    This updates the version in pyproject.toml, uv.lock and docs/index.md, adds a heading for it to CHANGELOG.md, then commits to a new bump_version_to_<version> branch and pushes it. 4. Create a pull request for the pushed branch, keeping the Bump version: <old> → <new> title. 5. Get the pull request approved and merge it.

Merging the pull request starts the release:

  1. The Version Bump merged workflow tags the merge commit as v<version>, creates the GitHub release with that version's CHANGELOG section as its notes, and starts the Publish Release workflow for the tag.
  2. Publish Release checks out the tag and:
    • publishes the documentation for the version with mike. A full release becomes the documentation's latest version; a prerelease (e.g. 2.1.0-rc.1) doesn't.
    • builds the wheel and source distribution and uploads them to PyPI. This job uses trusted publishing and runs in the Publish Release environment, so it waits until a repository maintainer approves it in the workflow run.

Don't create releases by hand: the version would not be updated in the files above. If publishing fails after the release was created, fix the cause and re-run the failed jobs, or start Publish Release again from the Actions tab (Run workflow, with the release tag, e.g. v2.0.0).

docs.title: Documentation Deploys
docs.text:
The documentation is published to GitHub Pages from the gh-pages branch with mike, one directory per version plus a dev version:

  • Every push to main rebuilds the dev documentation (the update-dev-docs job of the CI workflow).
  • Every release publishes its version, as described above.

The two kinds of deploy share a concurrency group, so only one pushes to gh-pages at a time. To preview the documentation locally, run docker compose run --rm --service-ports mkdocs and open http://localhost:8000.

docs.title: Repository Configuration
docs.text:
The release relies on these settings outside the repository:

  • GitHub environment Publish Release with required reviewers, which gates the PyPI upload. It needs no secrets.
  • PyPI trusted publisher for the gbq project: repository wayfair-incubator/gbq, workflow publish_release.yml, environment Publish Release.
  • GitHub environment Create Release, used by Version Bump merged. It needs no secrets: the release is created with the workflow's own GITHUB_TOKEN.
  • GitHub Pages serving the gh-pages branch.
  • Repository secret CODECOV_TOKEN for coverage uploads in CI.

docs.title: Continuous Integration Pipeline
docs.text:
The Continuous Integration (CI) Pipeline runs to confirm that the repository is in a good state. It will run when someone creates a pull request or when they push new commits to the branch for an existing pull request. The pipeline runs multiple different jobs that helps verify the state of the code.

This same pipeline also runs on the default branch when a maintainer merges a pull request.

docs.title: Lints
docs.text: The first set of jobs that run as part of the CI pipeline are linters that perform static analysis on the code. This includes: MyPy, Ruff, and Bandit.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
The next set of jobs run the unit tests using PyTest. The pipeline runs the tests cases across each supported version of Python to ensure compatibility.

For each run of the test cases, the job will record the test results and code coverage information. The pipeline uploads the code coverage information to CodeCov to ensure that a pull request doesn't significantly reduce the total code coverage percentage or introduce a large amount of code that is untested.

docs.title: Distribution Verification
docs.text: The next set of jobs build the wheel distribution, installs in into a virtual environment, and then runs Python to import the library version. This works as a smoke test to ensure that the library can be packaged correctly and used. The pipeline runs the tests cases across each supported version of Python to ensure compatibility.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
gbq requires Python 3.11 or later. Install it from PyPI:

python -m pip install gbq

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
gbq was developed internally at Wayfair to be used in a CD pipeline to create and update tables on Google BigQuery.

At Wayfair gbq is used with a BigQuery plugin which reads json schema files and updates the schemas on Google BigQuery.
